options.text: The small pair — the angle is the amount of opening, not the length of the blades
The large pair — its arms are much longer
Both the same — scissors always open to the same angle
options.diagnosis: Treats the angle as a fixed property of the object rather than of how far it is turned open.

options.text: Impossible to compare without a protractor
options.diagnosis: No turn-based intuition yet; wide-versus-narrow can be compared directly by eye or by overlaying.

questions.explanation: An angle measures the TURN between the arms. The small scissors are swung far apart (a wide turn), the big ones barely at all. Arm length only changes how big the picture is — not the angle.

questions.prompt: A set-square's right angle is rotated so that both its arms point diagonally. Is the angle still a right angle?

options.text: Yes — turning the whole angle does not change how open it is
No — a right angle needs one horizontal arm and one vertical arm
No — tilting it makes it acute
options.diagnosis: Perceives rotation as partially 'closing' the angle; the opening between the arms is unchanged.

options.text: Only if it is drawn on squared paper
options.diagnosis: Ties the property to the representation; an angle's size does not depend on the paper beneath it.

questions.explanation: Rotating an angle moves both arms together, so the opening between them stays exactly 90 degrees. A paper corner-tester still fits perfectly however the angle is tilted.

nodes.title: 3D Shapes, Boxes and Nets
nodes.description: A net is a flat pattern that folds up into a solid — unfold a toothpaste box and you are looking at its net. You will count faces, edges and corners of cubes and cuboids, decide which arrangements of squares fold into a cube and which do not, and sketch boxes on flat paper. This is the skill of packaging designers everywhere.
learning_outcomes: Can count faces, edges and vertices of cubes and cuboids
Can decide by mental folding whether a given arrangement of squares is a net of a cube
Can match a box to its net and mark which faces end up opposite each other
Can draw a simple net for an open or closed box

misconceptions.description: Thinks ANY arrangement of six squares folds into a cube — six squares is treated as the whole test.
misconceptions.signal: Accepts a 1×6 strip or a 2×3 block as a cube net without folding; counts squares and stops thinking.
misconceptions.remedy: Hand over cut-outs and have them actually fold: the 1×6 strip wraps around leaving two open holes and two doubled faces. Six squares is necessary but the ARRANGEMENT decides.

misconceptions.description: Counts only the faces that show in a drawing — a cube 'has 3 faces' (or 4), the hidden ones do not exist.
misconceptions.signal: Face counts match what is visible in the sketch; answers change depending on the picture used.
misconceptions.remedy: Stamp each face of a real dice or box with paint onto paper, counting the prints: six prints, always. Then revisit drawings and mark hidden faces with dotted shading.

misconceptions.description: Expects the net to LOOK like the solid — rejects valid cross-shaped cube nets because 'a cube is square, this is a plus sign'.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses the most compact/symmetric arrangement as 'the net'; calls the T and Z shaped nets wrong on sight.
misconceptions.remedy: Unfold several identical boxes along different edges to collect visibly different nets of the SAME box. A net records the unfolding path, not the solid's silhouette — there are 11 different cube nets!

real_world_hooks: Unfolding a toothpaste or mithai box flat
Designing a gift box for Diwali sweets
Dice: opposite faces of a dice always add to 7
Flattened cartons stacked at the kirana shop for recycling
teaching.video_search: nets of a cube folding boxes faces edges vertices class 5

questions.prompt: How many faces does a cube have?

options.diagnosis: Counted the corners (vertices) instead of the faces.
Counted the edges instead of the faces.

questions.explanation: A cube has 6 square faces (top, bottom, and 4 sides), 12 edges and 8 vertices. In a drawing only 3 faces show — the other 3 are hidden behind.

questions.prompt: Six squares are joined in one straight strip (1 × 6). Will this fold into a cube?

options.text: No — it wraps around the cube, doubling some faces and leaving two faces uncovered
Yes — it has exactly 6 squares, which is all a cube needs
Yes — any 6-square shape works if you fold it carefully enough
options.diagnosis: No mental (or physical) folding test performed; care cannot fix an impossible layout.

options.text: No — a cube's net needs 8 squares
options.diagnosis: Wrong face count for a cube; the issue with the strip is its arrangement, not the number 6.

questions.explanation: Fold the strip and it rolls around like a ring: four squares form the sides, then the last two land on faces already covered, while the two end holes stay open. Six squares are needed, but only certain arrangements (11 of them) fold into a cube.

questions.prompt: A sweet shop wants an OPEN box (no lid) shaped like a cube. How many square faces does its net need?

options.diagnosis: Included the lid — the box is open on top, so one face is deliberately missing.
Counted the corners of a cube instead of its faces.

questions.explanation: A closed cube has 6 faces; removing the lid leaves 5 — one base and four walls. Its net is 5 squares, for example a plus-sign shape with the centre square as the base.

nodes.title: Symmetry, Turns and Tiling Patterns
nodes.description: Some shapes look exactly the same after a quarter turn (90°) or a half turn (180°) — that is turning (rotational) symmetry, a cousin of mirror symmetry but not the same thing. Turns also build patterns: many rangoli, tile and border designs repeat a single motif by rotating it again and again. You will predict what a shape looks like after a turn and continue turn-based patterns.
learning_outcomes: Can state that a quarter turn is 90°, a half turn 180° and a full turn 360°
Can predict what a shape or letter looks like after a quarter or half turn
Can test whether a figure looks the same after a given turn, and distinguish this from mirror symmetry
Can continue and create tiling/border patterns built from repeated turns of one motif

misconceptions.description: Mixes up reflection and rotation — assumes a shape with a mirror line must also look the same after a turn, and turns figures by flipping them.
misconceptions.signal: Says E looks the same after a half turn 'because it is symmetric'; rotation tasks produce mirror images (b turned becomes d).
misconceptions.remedy: Physically contrast the two motions with one letter cut-out: FLIP the E across its mirror line (matches) versus TURN it 180° (upside-down E — does not match). One motion lifts the paper over; the other spins it flat.

misconceptions.description: Assumes a shape returns to itself after a half turn as long as it looks 'regular' or balanced.
misconceptions.signal: Claims triangles, hearts and the letter A all 'look the same upside down'; never actually rotates the figure.
misconceptions.remedy: Make trace-and-turn the required test: trace the figure, pin the centre, rotate the tracing 180° and see whether it truly matches. Balance to the eye is a guess; the tracing is evidence.

misconceptions.description: Confuses turn amounts — treats a quarter turn as 180° or as 'a little tilt', and half turns as full turns.
misconceptions.signal: Turns the figure the wrong amount in drawings; says a quarter turn brings a shape back to the start.
misconceptions.remedy: Link turns to the clock and the body: facing north, a quarter turn faces east (90°), another quarter faces south (180° in all). Four quarter turns — and only four — bring you home.

real_world_hooks: Rangoli and kolam motifs repeated by quarter turns
Fan blades and the wheel of a ship — same after part turns
Playing cards that look identical upside down
Floor tiling patterns in temples and railway stations
teaching.video_search: rotational symmetry half turn quarter turn patterns class 5

questions.prompt: A quarter turn is a turn of how many degrees?

options.diagnosis: Mapped 'quarter' to 25 as in 25 paise out of 100; a turn's whole is 360°, and a quarter of 360 is 90.
Halved a right angle instead — a quarter turn is a quarter of the full 360° turn, which is 90°, not 45°.

questions.explanation: A full turn is 360°. A quarter of it is 360 ÷ 4 = 90° — the turn from facing north to facing east, or the clock's minute hand moving 15 minutes.

questions.prompt: The letter 'b' is given a half turn (rotated 180°). What does it look like now?

options.diagnosis: Flipped the letter top-to-bottom (a reflection in a horizontal mirror) instead of turning it.

questions.explanation: A half turn spins the letter around its centre: the stick that pointed up now points down, and the bump swaps sides — 'b' becomes 'q'. A mirror flip would give 'd', which is a different motion.

questions.prompt: A border pattern repeats one arrow tile, giving it a quarter turn each time: UP, RIGHT, DOWN, LEFT, ... What is the 5th tile?

options.text: UP — after four quarter turns the arrow is back to the start
RIGHT — a quarter turn from LEFT flips it to the opposite side
LEFT — the last tile simply repeats
options.diagnosis: Copied the previous item instead of applying the turn rule again; the pattern's rule is 'turn', not 'stay'.

options.text: Any direction — the tiles are placed randomly
options.diagnosis: The rotation rule was never spotted; check each step: every arrow is the previous one turned 90° clockwise.

questions.explanation: Each tile is the previous one turned 90°: up → right → down → left → up. Four quarter turns make a full 360°, so the 5th tile matches the 1st. Turning LEFT by only a quarter gives UP; jumping to RIGHT would need a half turn.

nodes.title: Area and Perimeter of Rectangles (Formulas)
nodes.description: Counting squares one by one is slow — for rectangles, multiplication does it instantly: area = length × width, because the squares sit in equal rows. Perimeter has its own shortcut: 2 × (length + width). The two formulas answer two different questions (covering vs surrounding), use different units (square cm vs cm), and mixing them up is the classic trap.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the area of a rectangle as length × width and justify it with rows of squares
Can compute the perimeter of a rectangle as 2 × (length + width)
Can attach the correct units: square units for area, length units for perimeter
Can find a missing side given the area or perimeter, and compare rectangles with equal perimeter

misconceptions.description: Swaps the formulas — multiplies sides for perimeter or adds-and-doubles for area; treats 'area and perimeter' as one interchangeable idea.
misconceptions.signal: The right numbers go into the wrong formula; answers to 'fencing' problems come out in square metres.
misconceptions.remedy: Re-derive each formula from its meaning every time for a while: area = rows of squares (3 rows of 9 squares → 3 × 9); perimeter = walk around the boundary (9 + 4 + 9 + 4). The question 'cover it or go around it?' picks the formula.

misconceptions.description: Believes rectangles with the same perimeter must have the same area (and same area means same perimeter).
misconceptions.signal: Given a fixed fence length, says all possible plots 'hold the same amount'; skips computing areas separately.
misconceptions.remedy: Fix a 24-unit loop of string and build 1×11, 4×8 and 6×6 rectangles on a pegboard, recording area each time (11, 32, 36). Same fence, wildly different areas — squarer is roomier.

misconceptions.description: Ignores or swaps units — reports area in cm and perimeter in square cm, or drops units entirely.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 'area = 36 cm'; unit choice looks random and survives unchallenged.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie the unit to the measuring object: perimeter is measured by laying down 1 cm STICKS (cm), area by covering with 1 cm SQUARES (sq cm). Require the unit-object to be named with every answer.

real_world_hooks: Fencing a plot vs buying grass to cover it
Tiles for the kitchen floor vs skirting along its walls
A farmer choosing the roomiest field shape for a fixed fence
Framing a photo (perimeter) vs the glass to cover it (area)

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its AREA?

options.diagnosis: Added the two sides once (9 + 4); neither the area nor the perimeter recipe was completed.

questions.explanation: Area = length × width = 9 × 4 = 36 square cm — four rows of nine unit squares. 26 cm is the perimeter, 2 × (9 + 4); and area must carry SQUARE units because it counts squares.

questions.prompt: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 7 m wide. How much fencing is needed for its PERIMETER?

options.diagnosis: Computed length + width but forgot to double it — only half the boundary was walked.
Doubled only the length (2 × 12); the two widths went missing.

questions.explanation: Perimeter = 2 × (12 + 7) = 2 × 19 = 38 m. Multiplying 12 × 7 = 84 gives the area in square metres — how much ground the garden covers, not the fence around it.

questions.prompt: A farmer has exactly 24 m of fencing. Which rectangular plot gives her the MOST area: 1 m × 11 m, 4 m × 8 m, or 6 m × 6 m?

options.text: 6 m × 6 m — its area is 36 sq m, beating 32 and 11
All three hold the same area — they use the same 24 m of fence
1 m × 11 m — the longest side wins
options.diagnosis: Maximised one dimension only; a long thin strip encloses very little ground.

options.text: 4 m × 8 m — a square does not count as a rectangle
options.diagnosis: A square IS a rectangle (all right angles, opposite sides equal) — excluding it discards the best option.

questions.explanation: All three have perimeter 24 m, but the areas differ: 1 × 11 = 11, 4 × 8 = 32, 6 × 6 = 36 sq m. Equal perimeter does not mean equal area — the squarer the rectangle, the more it encloses.

nodes.title: Volume Intuition with Unit Cubes
nodes.description: Volume measures how much space something fills, and we measure it by counting unit cubes — including the ones hidden inside and underneath. A box packs cubes in layers: cubes per layer × number of layers. Rearranging the same cubes into a tower or a slab changes the shape but never the volume.
learning_outcomes: Can find the volume of a cube-built solid by counting unit cubes, including hidden ones
Can use layers to count: cubes in one layer × number of layers
Can explain that rearranging cubes changes shape but not volume
Can compare volumes of two cube buildings and order containers by how much they hold

misconceptions.description: Counts only the cubes visible in a drawing — hidden and underneath cubes do not exist.
misconceptions.signal: A 2×2×2 stack drawn on paper is counted as 7 (or fewer); answers change with the viewing angle.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the drawn solid from real cubes, count by dismantling, and compare with the drawing count. Then practise 'X-ray counting': for each visible column, ask how many cubes stand in it top to bottom.

misconceptions.description: Stops at one layer — treats the base layer (or the taller-looking shape) as the whole volume.
misconceptions.signal: Multi-layer boxes get single-layer answers; 'taller' is declared 'more' without counting.
misconceptions.remedy: Fill a small open box with cube layers one at a time, pausing to record the running total: 12, 24, ... Volume = one layer × layers becomes something watched, not memorised.

misconceptions.description: Believes rearranging changes the amount — 12 cubes as a tall tower 'is more' than the same 12 as a flat slab (non-conservation).
misconceptions.signal: Judges quantity by height or spread; refuses to accept equality without recounting; wants to weigh them 'to be sure'.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student personally rebuild the SAME 12 cubes from tower to slab and back, counting each time. The cubes never left their hands — nothing was added or removed, so the volume is unchanged.

real_world_hooks: Stacking sugar cubes or Maggi packets into a carton
How many small mithai boxes fit in the shop's big carton
Bricks stacked in layers at a building site
Water displaced when you drop stones in a measuring jug

questions.prompt: A box is filled with 2 layers of cubes. Each layer has 3 rows of 4 cubes. How many cubes are in the box?

options.diagnosis: Added 3 + 4 = 7 and doubled it — the layer needs 3 × 4 cubes, not 3 + 4.
Added all three numbers (3 + 4 + 2); the structure of layers-of-arrays was not used.

questions.explanation: One layer holds 3 × 4 = 12 cubes. Two layers hold 12 × 2 = 24 cubes. Layer count × cubes per layer is the fast way to count a box full of cubes.

questions.prompt: A drawing shows a 2 × 2 × 2 cube stack. Ravi counts 7 cubes because that is how many he can see. How many cubes are really there?

options.diagnosis: Counted one 2 × 2 face only; the stack is two such layers deep.
Counted the six faces of the big cube instead of the small cubes inside it.

questions.explanation: The stack is 2 layers of 2 × 2 = 4 cubes, so 4 × 2 = 8. One cube hides at the back bottom corner where the drawing cannot show it — hidden cubes still count.

questions.prompt: Meena builds a tall tower from 12 cubes. Arjun uses his own 12 identical cubes to make a flat 3 × 4 slab. Who has used more material?

options.text: Both the same — 12 cubes is 12 cubes, however they are arranged
Meena — the tower is taller, so it must be more
Arjun — the slab spreads over more of the table
options.diagnosis: Judged by footprint area; spreading out is the flip side of height, and neither changes the count.

options.text: Impossible to tell without weighing both

questions.explanation: Each build uses exactly 12 unit cubes, so the volumes are equal. Height and spread trade off against each other; rearranging cubes never creates or destroys any. (Weighing would just confirm 12 = 12.)

nodes.title: Interpreting Tables, Bar Graphs and Simple Pie Charts
nodes.description: Data answers questions — if you read it correctly. You will pull values out of tables, read scaled bar graphs precisely (including part-divisions), and interpret simple pie charts where a slice is a fraction of the total. The golden rules: check the scale, and remember a pie slice is a fraction — its actual count depends on the total.
learning_outcomes: Can extract and compare values from a data table, including finding least and greatest
Can read bar graphs with scaled axes, including bars ending between gridlines
Can interpret a simple pie chart by applying its fractions (half, quarter) to the stated total
Can answer multi-step questions combining two or more readings from one display

misconceptions.description: Reads a pie slice's fraction as a raw count — 'half the circle' becomes '50 people' whatever the total is.
misconceptions.signal: Answers to pie-chart questions are 50, 25 and similar percent-flavoured numbers regardless of the stated total.
misconceptions.remedy: Always write the total above the pie first, then compute each slice AS a fraction OF that total: half of 60 is 30. Compare two pies with equal slices but different totals (half of 60 vs half of 200) to break the '50' reflex.

misconceptions.description: Ignores the axis scale on bar graphs — counts divisions as if each were 1, and rounds bars that end between gridlines to the nearest line.
misconceptions.signal: Bar readings match the gridline count, not the data; half-divisions are silently rounded away.
misconceptions.remedy: Keep the scale-check ritual ('1 division = __') and practise on bars deliberately drawn to end mid-division: the reading is divisions × scale, including the half.

misconceptions.description: Compares multi-digit values in a table by their first digits or by length of the written word, declaring 9 greater than 15.
misconceptions.signal: 'Least/greatest' answers contradict the numbers; single-digit entries beat teens in the student's ranking.
misconceptions.remedy: Route the comparison through place value: line the column's values up right-justified and compare digit counts first. Data reading is only as good as the number comparison underneath it.

real_world_hooks: Runs per over charts from an IPL match
Library register: books borrowed each day of the week
A pie chart of how a family's monthly budget is split
Rainfall or temperature tables from the newspaper

questions.prompt: A table shows books borrowed from the library: Mon 12, Tue 15, Wed 9, Thu 21. On which day were the FEWEST books borrowed?

options.diagnosis: Picked the greatest value — the question asks for the fewest; 'least/most' words need flagging before reading.
Compared 15 and 9 by their first digits (1 < 9) and judged 15 smaller; digit count decides first.

questions.explanation: Compare the four values: 9 < 12 < 15 < 21, so Wednesday (9 books) is the fewest. A single-digit number is always less than any two-digit number, even though 9 is a 'big' digit.

questions.prompt: In a bar graph of favourite sports, each division stands for 10 children. The kabaddi bar rises 4 and a half divisions. How many children chose kabaddi?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by the scale but dropped the half division — that half stands for 5 real children.
Rounded the bar up to the next gridline before scaling; the graph must be read exactly.

questions.explanation: 4.5 divisions × 10 children per division = 45 children. The half division is data too: it represents 5 children, not something to round away.

questions.prompt: A pie chart of 60 students' favourite fruit shows: half the circle for mango, a quarter for banana, a quarter for apple. How many students chose mango?

options.diagnosis: Computed a quarter of 60 instead of half — the slice fractions were swapped.
Reported the total number of students; the slice's fraction was never applied to it.

questions.explanation: The mango slice is half the circle, and half OF the 60 students is 30. A pie slice is a fraction, not a count — the same half-circle would mean 100 students if the total were 200.
